claim: Hepatocytes from obese mice displayed significantly diminished SOCE as a result of impaired STIM1 translocation.
source: Here, we show that hepatocytes from obese mice displayed significantly diminished SOCE as a result of impaired STIM1 translocation, which was associated with aberrant STIM1 O-GlycNAcylation.
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements showing reduced SOCE in Lepob/ob hepatocytes (Figure 1A), confocal imaging showing impaired STIM1 translocation (Figure 1C-H), and TIRF microscopy (Figure 1I-J).

claim: Impaired STIM1 translocation in obese hepatocytes was associated with aberrant STIM1 O-GlycNAcylation.
source: Here, we show that hepatocytes from obese mice displayed significantly diminished SOCE as a result of impaired STIM1 translocation, which was associated with aberrant STIM1 O-GlycNAcylation.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation showing increased O-GlcNAcylation of STIM1 in Lepob/ob hepatocytes (Figure 2C-D), and WGA pull-down experiments (Figure 2D).

claim: Primary hepatocytes deficient in STIM1 exhibited elevated cellular stress.
source: Primary hepatocytes deficient in STIM1 exhibited elevated cellular stress as well as impaired insulin action, increased glucose production and lipid droplet accumulation.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing increased phosphorylation of JNK and eIF2α in STIM1-deficient hepatocytes (Figure 3B).

claim: Primary hepatocytes deficient in STIM1 exhibited impaired insulin action.
source: Primary hepatocytes deficient in STIM1 exhibited elevated cellular stress as well as impaired insulin action, increased glucose production and lipid droplet accumulation.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing decreased phosphorylation of IRβ and AKT in response to insulin in STIM1-deficient hepatocytes (Figure 3C).

claim: Primary hepatocytes deficient in STIM1 exhibited increased glucose production.
source: Primary hepatocytes deficient in STIM1 exhibited elevated cellular stress as well as impaired insulin action, increased glucose production and lipid droplet accumulation.
evidence: Supported by glucose production assay showing higher glucose output in STIM1-deficient hepatocytes (Figure 3E).

claim: Primary hepatocytes deficient in STIM1 exhibited lipid droplet accumulation.
source: Primary hepatocytes deficient in STIM1 exhibited elevated cellular stress as well as impaired insulin action, increased glucose production and lipid droplet accumulation.
evidence: Supported by BODIPY staining showing increased lipid droplet accumulation in STIM1-deficient hepatocytes (Figure 3D).

claim: Mice with acute liver deletion of STIM1 displayed systemic glucose intolerance.
source: Additionally, mice with acute liver deletion of STIM1 displayed systemic glucose intolerance.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test showing impaired glucose tolerance in mice with acute STIM1 deletion (Figure 3J).

claim: Over-expression of STIM1 in obese mice led to increased SOCE.
source: Conversely, over-expression of STIM1 in obese mice led to increased SOCE, which was sufficient to improve systemic glucose tolerance.
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements showing increased SOCE in Lepob/ob hepatocytes overexpressing STIM1-YFP (Figure 4G).

claim: Over-expression of STIM1 in obese mice was sufficient to improve systemic glucose tolerance.
source: Conversely, over-expression of STIM1 in obese mice led to increased SOCE, which was sufficient to improve systemic glucose tolerance.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test showing improved glucose tolerance in Lepob/ob mice overexpressing STIM1-YFP (Figure 5D).

claim: The initial rise in cytosolic Ca2+ induced by Tg was significantly lower in hepatocytes isolated from obese animals compared with WT cells.
source: In agreement with earlier reports (Arruda et al., 2014) the initial rise in cytosolic Ca2+ induced by Tg, which reflects the ER Ca2+ content, was significantly lower in hepatocytes isolated from obese animals compared with WT cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements (Figure 1A) and cited previous work (Arruda et al., 2014).

claim: Ca2+ entry in primary hepatocytes from obese mice was markedly reduced relative to control cells.
source: As depicted in Figure 1A, the Ca2+ entry in primary hepatocytes from obese mice was markedly reduced relative to control cells.
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements showing reduced SOCE in Lepob/ob hepatocytes (Figure 1A).

claim: 2-apb completely blocked Ca2+ influx in both WT and Lepob/ob genotypes.
source: To further confirm that the observed Ca2+ entry was mediated by SOCE, we added the SOCE inhibitor 2-apb, which completely blocked Ca2+ influx in both genotypes (Figure 1A, dotted lines).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements in the presence of 2-apb (Figure 1A).

claim: Impaired SOCE in steatotic hepatocytes from Zucker rats has been reported.
source: This finding is consistent with a report of impaired SOCE in the steatotic hepatocytes from Zucker rats (Wilson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2015.

claim: No differences in expression of Orai1 were detected in the livers of mice with genetic or high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, we did not detect differences in expression of Orai1 in the livers of mice with genetic or high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Despite a modest increase in the mRNA levels of stim1 and stim2, protein levels of STIM1, STIM2 and Orai1 remained unchanged in the livers of mice with both genetic and diet induced obesity.
source: Despite a modest increase in the mRNA levels of stim1 and stim2, protein levels of STIM1, STIM2 and Orai1 remained unchanged in the livers of mice with both genetic and diet induced obesity (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and western blot analysis (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Phospho-JNK (pJNK), a marker of inflammatory stress, was increased in the livers of obese animals.
source: However, phospho-JNK (pJNK), a marker of inflammatory stress (Hirosumi et al., 2002) and phospho-Calmodulin kinase (pCaMKII), a marker of elevated cytosolic Ca2+ (Ozcan et al., 2012), were increased in the livers of obese animals (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and citations to Hirosumi et al., 2002 and Ozcan et al., 2012.

claim: Phospho-Calmodulin kinase (pCaMKII), a marker of elevated cytosolic Ca2+, was increased in the livers of obese animals.
source: However, phospho-JNK (pJNK), a marker of inflammatory stress (Hirosumi et al., 2002) and phospho-Calmodulin kinase (pCaMKII), a marker of elevated cytosolic Ca2+ (Ozcan et al., 2012), were increased in the livers of obese animals (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and citation to Ozcan et al., 2012.

claim: STIM1 was evenly distributed in the ER membrane of resting cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, while STIM1 was evenly distributed in the ER membrane of resting cells, Tg treatment led to a dramatic translocation to areas of the ER membrane in close proximity with the PM.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of STIM1 in primary hepatocytes (Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Tg treatment led to a dramatic translocation of STIM1 to areas of the ER membrane in close proximity with the PM.
source: As shown in Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, while STIM1 was evenly distributed in the ER membrane of resting cells, Tg treatment led to a dramatic translocation to areas of the ER membrane in close proximity with the PM.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of STIM1 in primary hepatocytes (Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: STIM1 translocation in response to Tg was observed within 5–10 min of Tg treatment and persisted for 30 min.
source: This effect was observed within 5–10 min of Tg treatment and persisted for 30 min.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of STIM1 at different time points (Figure 1C and D).

claim: In cells from obese (Lepob/ob) mice, STIM1 distribution at baseline was punctate throughout the entire ER.
source: However, in cells from obese (Lepob/ob) mice, STIM1 distribution at baseline was punctate throughout the entire ER (Figure 1D and quantified in Figure 1E), and its translocation to areas of ER/PM junction in response to Tg was dramatically impaired.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of STIM1 in Lepob/ob hepatocytes (Figure 1D) and quantification (Figure 1E).

claim: STIM1 translocation to areas of ER/PM junction in response to Tg was dramatically impaired in cells from obese (Lepob/ob) mice.
source: However, in cells from obese (Lepob/ob) mice, STIM1 distribution at baseline was punctate throughout the entire ER (Figure 1D and quantified in Figure 1E), and its translocation to areas of ER/PM junction in response to Tg was dramatically impaired.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of STIM1 in Lepob/ob hepatocytes (Figure 1D) and quantification (Figure 1H).

claim: In WT cells, Tg treatment increased the number of high-intensity pixels, indicating the formation of punctate structures, which represent oligomerization of STIM proteins.
source: As shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, in WT cells, Tg treatment increased the number of high-intensity pixels, indicating the formation of the punctate structures, which represent oligomerization of STIM proteins.
evidence: Supported by pixel intensity analysis of confocal images (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Hepatocytes derived from obese mice displayed higher intensity pixel counts at baseline with no further increase following Tg treatment.
source: In contrast, hepatocytes derived from obese mice displayed higher intensity pixel counts at baseline with no further increase following Tg treatment.
evidence: Supported by pixel intensity analysis of confocal images (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: In WT cells, Tg treatment increased the signal intensity at the edge of the cell and decreased it in the cytosol.
source: In WT cells, Tg treatment increased the signal intensity at the edge of the cell and decreased it in the cytosol, quantified as the STIM1 ratio between these compartments (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by line graph analysis and edge/cytosol ratio quantification (Figure 1G and 1H).

claim: In hepatocytes from obese mice, the average signal intensity at baseline was higher than in WT cells, and did not change significantly in response to Tg.
source: In hepatocytes from obese mice, the average signal intensity at baseline was higher than in WT cells, and did not change significantly in response to Tg (Figure 1H), indicating that STIM1 translocation is markedly defective in these cells.
evidence: Supported by edge/cytosol ratio quantification (Figure 1H).

claim: In WT cells, Tg treatment induced STIM1 puncta formation and accumulation in areas close to the PM.
source: As shown in Figure 1I, in WT cells Tg treatment induced STIM1 puncta formation and accumulation in areas close to the PM.
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy images (Figure 1I).

claim: STIM1 puncta formation and accumulation in areas close to the PM in response to Tg was diminished in cells derived from obese animals.
source: This response was diminished in cells derived from obese animals (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy images (Figure 1J).

claim: After 3 and 5 weeks of HFD, STIM1 showed some degree of translocation towards the plasma membrane in resting cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, after 3 and 5 weeks of HFD, STIM1 showed some degree of translocation towards the plasma membrane in resting cells, indicating that short term HFD exposure is sufficient to trigger ER Ca2+ release, the driving force for STIM1 translocation.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of STIM1 in hepatocytes from HFD-fed mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).

claim: At 3 weeks HFD, STIM1 translocation stimulated by Tg was not significantly impaired compared with cells derived from chow fed animals.
source: Additionally, at 3 weeks HFD, STIM1 translocation stimulated by Tg was not significantly impaired compared with cells derived from chow fed animals.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of STIM1 in hepatocytes from HFD-fed mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).

claim: The defect in STIM1 translocation induced by Tg was apparent in cells isolated from mice fed a HFD for 5 weeks and was more pronounced after 7 and 11 weeks of HFD.
source: However, the defect in STIM1 translocation induced by Tg was apparent in cells isolated from mice fed a HFD for 5 weeks and was more pronounced after 7 and 11 weeks of HFD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of STIM1 in hepatocytes from HFD-fed mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).

claim: Defective STIM1 translocation may be a common feature of obesity in independent experimental models (Lepob/ob and HFD).
source: These data support that defective STIM1 translocation may be a common feature of obesity in independent experimental models (Lepob/ob and HFD) and that this phenotype occurs independent of blood glucose levels and prior to the emergence of marked hyper-insulinemia and insulin resistance found in obesity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data from both Lepob/ob and HFD models (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Defective STIM1 translocation occurs independent of blood glucose levels and prior to the emergence of marked hyper-insulinemia and insulin resistance found in obesity.
source: These data support that defective STIM1 translocation may be a common feature of obesity in independent experimental models (Lepob/ob and HFD) and that this phenotype occurs independent of blood glucose levels and prior to the emergence of marked hyper-insulinemia and insulin resistance found in obesity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by metabolic measurements in HFD-fed mice at different time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).

claim: STIM2 is expressed at a lower level than STIM1 in hepatocytes.
source: In hepatocytes, STIM2 is expressed at a lower level than STIM1 (López et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2001), however it was detectable both by staining and by western blot analysis.
evidence: Supported by citations to López et al., 2012 and Williams et al., 2001, and western blot data (Figure 1B).

claim: Upon Tg-induced store depletion, STIM2 translocated to areas close to the PM in both WT cells and Lepob/ob cells.
source: Upon Tg-induced store depletion, we observed a marked STIM2 translocation to areas close to the PM in both WT cells and Lepob/ob cells, however the degree of translocation in Lepob/ob cells was less pronounced than in WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of STIM2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: The degree of STIM2 translocation in Lepob/ob cells was less pronounced than in WT cells.
source: Upon Tg-induced store depletion, we observed a marked STIM2 translocation to areas close to the PM in both WT cells and Lepob/ob cells, however the degree of translocation in Lepob/ob cells was less pronounced than in WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of STIM2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: The obesity-related defect in STIM2 translocation was present but less dramatic than that observed for STIM1.
source: Thus, the obesity-related defect in STIM2 translocation was present but less dramatic than that observed for STIM1.
evidence: Supported by comparison of STIM1 and STIM2 translocation data (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: Defective SOCE in primary hepatocytes from obese mice is predominantly related to aberrant STIM1 puncta formation and inefficient STIM1 re-localization from the bulk ER membrane to ER/PM junction areas after ER Ca2+ store depletion.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that defective SOCE in primary hepatocytes from obese mice is predominantly related to aberrant STIM1 puncta formation and inefficient STIM1 re-localization from the bulk ER membrane to ER/PM junction areas after ER Ca2+ store depletion.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging, TIRF microscopy, and calcium imaging data (Figure 1).

claim: Phosphorylation of STIM1 at Ser621 and Ser575 regulate its interaction with the microtubule plus-end-tracking protein EB1, enabling STIM1 to move in the ER membrane.
source: Phosphorylation of STIM1 at Ser621 and Ser575 regulate its interaction with the microtubule plus-end-tracking protein EB1, enabling STIM1 to move in the ER membrane (Pozo-Guisado et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pozo-Guisado et al., 2013.

claim: Phosphorylation of STIM1 at Ser621 and Ser575 was increased in liver lysates from obese mice.
source: Surprisingly however, we found that phosphorylation of STIM1 at Ser621 and Ser575 was actually increased in liver lysates from obese mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 2A).

claim: Lack of phosphorylation at Ser621 and Ser575 does not underlie the defective translocation of STIM1 in obesity.
source: This indicates that lack of phosphorylation at these residues does not underlie the defective translocation of STIM1, and suggests that hepatic STIM1 may be released from EB1 in the basal state, potentially as a response to the decreased ER Ca2+ level observed in hepatocytes from obese mice.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing increased phosphorylation (Figure 2A) and logical inference.

claim: Global O-GlcNAcylation was higher in hepatocytes derived from obese animals compared with their controls.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, and in agreement with previous observations (Baldini et al., 2016), global O-GlcNAcylation was higher in hepatocytes derived from obese animals compared with their controls.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 2B) and citation to Baldini et al., 2016.

claim: STIM1 was present among the OglcNAcylated proteins and it was more abundant in cells from obese mice.
source: We found that STIM1 was present among the OglcNAcylated proteins and it was more abundant in cells from obese mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation of O-GlcNAc-modified proteins followed by STIM1 immunoblotting (Figure 2C).

claim: STIM1 was detected in the pool of proteins modified by O-GlcNac at higher levels in samples derived from obese animals relative to WT controls.
source: Following precipitation with streptavidin-conjugated magnetic beads, STIM1 was detected in the pool of proteins modified by O-GlcNac at higher levels in samples derived from obese animals relative to WT controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by WGA pull-down followed by STIM1 immunoblotting (Figure 2D).

claim: OGT precipitates with STIM1 in hepatocytes derived from obese animals.
source: As shown in Figure 2E, OGT precipitates with STIM1 in hepatocytes derived from obese animals, indicating that OGT and STIM1 exist in a complex in obesity, consistent with higher levels of O-GlcNac-modified STIM1 in this condition.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation of STIM1 followed by OGT immunoblotting (Figure 2E).

claim: STIM1 was progressively modified by O-GlcNac in the HFD context starting at 3 weeks on HFD.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, STIM1 was progressively modified by O-GlcNac in this context starting at 3 weeks on HFD.
evidence: Supported by WGA pull-down of STIM1 from hepatocytes of HFD-fed mice at different time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Overexpression of OGT strongly increased global protein modification with O-GlcNac.
source: As expected, overexpression of OGT strongly increased global protein modification with O-GlcNac (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of O-GlcNAc in OGT-overexpressing cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: STIM1-Flag showed enhanced O-GlcNAc modification in OGT overexpressing cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation of STIM1-Flag with a Flag specific antibody demonstrated its enhanced O-GlcNAc modification in OGT overexpressing cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation of STIM1-Flag followed by O-GlcNAc immunoblotting (Figure 2F).

claim: STIM1 is able to directly bind to OGT in Hepa1-6 cells overexpressing STIM1-Flag and OGT.
source: Additionally, STIM1 is able to directly bind to OGT in this cell model (Figure 2F), similar to what we observed in hepatocytes derived from obese animals (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation of STIM1-Flag followed by OGT immunoblotting (Figure 2F).

claim: STIM1 puncta formation and translocation following Tg treatment was markedly impaired in cells overexpressing OGT compared with control cells.
source: These experiments showed that STIM1 puncta formation and translocation following Tg treatment was markedly impaired in cells overexpressing OGT compared with control cells (Figure 2G,H and I).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of STIM1 in OGT-overexpressing cells (Figure 2G, H, and I).

claim: Overexpression of OGT led to a significant impairment in SOCE compared with the controls.
source: Additionally, overexpression of OGT led to a significant impairment in SOCE compared with the controls (Figure 2J), with no significant differences in the response to Tg (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by Fluo-4 calcium measurements in OGT-overexpressing cells (Figure 2J).

claim: Down-regulation of OGT resulted in increased STIM1 translocation capacity compared with cells expressing a scrambled shRNA.
source: As shown in Figure 2M and N, down-regulation of OGT resulted in increased STIM1 translocation capacity compared with cells expressing a scrambled shRNA.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of STIM1 in Lepob/ob hepatocytes with OGT knockdown (Figure 2M and N).

claim: Increased modification of STIM1 by OglcNAc could, at least in part, underlie defective STIM1 translocation and reduced hepatic SOCE in the context of obesity.
source: Taken together these data indicate that increased modification of STIM1 by OglcNAc could, at least in part, underlie defective STIM1 translocation and reduced hepatic SOCE in the context of obesity.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing O-GlcNAcylation of STIM1 in obesity, OGT overexpression impairing STIM1 function, and OGT knockdown rescuing STIM1 translocation (Figure 2).

claim: Primary hepatocytes derived from stim1ΔLIVER mice displayed lower ER Ca2+ content compared to controls (stim1fl/fl).
source: Primary hepatocytes derived from stim1ΔLIVER mice displayed lower ER Ca2+ content and absence of Tg-triggered SOCE compared to controls (stim1fl/fl) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements (Figure 3A).

claim: Primary hepatocytes derived from stim1ΔLIVER mice displayed absence of Tg-triggered SOCE compared to controls (stim1fl/fl).
source: Primary hepatocytes derived from stim1ΔLIVER mice displayed lower ER Ca2+ content and absence of Tg-triggered SOCE compared to controls (stim1fl/fl) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements (Figure 3A).

claim: Hepa 1–6 cells in which STIM1 expression was down regulated showed markedly blunted SOCE.
source: Similarly, Hepa 1–6 cells in which STIM1 expression was down regulated showed markedly blunted SOCE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements in STIM1 knockdown cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

claim: In stim1fl/fl control cells, treatment with Tg induced phosphorylation of JNK and eIF2α at 30 min followed by a decrease in phosphorylation levels back to baseline after 90 min.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, in stim1fl/fl control cells, treatment with Tg induced phosphorylation of JNK and eIF2α at 30 min followed by a decrease in phosphorylation levels back to baseline after 90 min.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of stress markers in stim1fl/fl hepatocytes (Figure 3B).

claim: In STIM1-deficient cells, the phosphorylation of JNK and eIF2α was enhanced at baseline.
source: However, in STIM1-deficient cells, the phosphorylation of JNK and eIF2α was enhanced at baseline and these cells displayed a stronger and more persistent response to Tg, with stress markers only returning to basal levels at 120 min.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of stress markers in stim1ΔLIVER hepatocytes (Figure 3B).

claim: STIM1-deficient cells displayed a stronger and more persistent response to Tg, with stress markers only returning to basal levels at 120 min.
source: However, in STIM1-deficient cells, the phosphorylation of JNK and eIF2α was enhanced at baseline and these cells displayed a stronger and more persistent response to Tg, with stress markers only returning to basal levels at 120 min.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of stress markers in stim1ΔLIVER hepatocytes (Figure 3B).

claim: Suppression of STIM2 alone did not alter the cellular response to Tg.
source: Interestingly, suppression of STIM2 alone did not alter the cellular response to Tg (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of stress markers in STIM2 knockdown cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Absence of core components of SOCE leads to elevated and prolonged stress responses in hepatocytes.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that absence of core components of SOCE leads to elevated and prolonged stress responses in hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of stress markers in STIM1-deficient hepatocytes (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Primary hepatocytes isolated from stim1ΔLIVER mice maintained on HFD showed higher levels of glucose production stimulated by the gluconeogenesis substrates glycerol, pyruvate and glutamine compared to stim1fl/fl derived hepatocytes.
source: Additionally, primary hepatocytes isolated from stim1ΔLIVER mice maintained on HFD showed higher levels of glucose production stimulated by the gluconeogenesis substrates glycerol, pyruvate and glutamine compared to stim1fl/fl derived hepatocytes (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by glucose production assay (Figure 3E).

claim: STIM2-deficient cells retained normal insulin responsiveness.
source: In agreement with our finding that STIM2 suppression does not amplify stress responses, we found that STIM2-deficient cells retained normal insulin responsiveness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of insulin signaling in STIM2 knockdown cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).

claim: Animals with inducible STIM1/2 whole body deficiency exhibit increased lipid accumulation in multiple tissues such as skeletal muscle, heart and liver, as a consequence of impaired lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation.
source: Recently, it has been shown that SOCE may regulate lipid metabolism (Maus et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2015) and animals with inducible STIM1/2 whole body deficiency exhibit increased lipid accumulation in multiple tissues such as skeletal muscle, heart and liver, as a consequence of impaired lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation (Maus et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maus et al., 2017 and Wilson et al., 2015.

claim: Primary hepatocytes isolated from stim1ΔLIVER mice showed modestly increased accumulation of lipid droplets at baseline and after incubation with 1 mM oleic acid and 40 µM of palmitic acid.
source: We observed that primary hepatocytes isolated from stim1ΔLIVER mice showed modestly increased accumulation of lipid droplets at baseline and after incubation with 1 mM oleic acid and 40 µM of palmitic acid (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by BODIPY staining of lipid droplets (Figure 3D).

claim: On a chow diet, stim1ΔLIVER mice gained weight equivalently to stim1fl/fl mice.
source: On a chow diet, stim1ΔLIVER mice gained weight equivalently to stim1fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) and did not exhibit alterations in glucose tolerance and triglyceride content (Tg) (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).

claim: On a chow diet, stim1ΔLIVER mice did not exhibit alterations in glucose tolerance and triglyceride content.
source: On a chow diet, stim1ΔLIVER mice gained weight equivalently to stim1fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) and did not exhibit alterations in glucose tolerance and triglyceride content (Tg) (data not shown).
evidence: Stated in the text but data not shown.

claim: In HFD-fed mice, the weight gain was similar between stim1ΔLIVER and stim1fl/fl genotypes.
source: In the HFD-fed mice, the weight gain was similar between genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).

claim: At 6 weeks on a HFD, stim1ΔLIVER animals showed a mild, but significant, glucose intolerance compared with the stim1fl/fl controls.
source: Interestingly, at 6 weeks on a HFD, we observed a mild, but significant, glucose intolerance in the stim1ΔLIVER animals compared with the stim1fl/fl controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).

claim: At 6 weeks on HFD, insulin sensitivity was impaired in stim1ΔLIVER animals.
source: Additionally, at this time point, insulin sensitivity was impaired (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo insulin signaling measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).

claim: In long term HFD (20 weeks), the differences in glucose intolerance, insulin signaling and Tg content between stim1fl/fl and stim1ΔLIVER groups were very mild and did not reach statistical significance.
source: In long term HFD (20 weeks), the differences in glucose intolerance, insulin signaling and Tg content between stim1fl/fl and stim1ΔLIVER groups were very mild and did not reach statistical significance (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F,G and H).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test, insulin signaling, and triglyceride measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, G, and H).

claim: stim1ΔLIVER animals showed higher content of microvesicular steatosis compared with controls where the majority of the lipid droplets are presented as large droplets.
source: Interestingly, although we haven't observed overall changes in lipid accumulation in the liver specific STIM1 deficient animals, we have noticed that these animals showed higher content of microvesicular steatosis compared with controls where the majority of the lipid droplets are presented as large droplets (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of liver sections (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I).

claim: Adenoviral delivery of Alb;Cre recombinase resulted in ~60% deletion of hepatic STIM1.
source: Adenoviral delivery of Alb;Cre recombinase resulted in ~60% deletion of hepatic STIM1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 3G).

claim: There was no compensatory upregulation of STIM2 or Orai1 following acute deletion of STIM1.
source: Importantly, there was no compensatory upregulation of STIM2 or Orai1 in this setting.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 3G).

claim: One week after adenovirus administration, the acute deletion of STIM1 resulted in significantly higher fasting glucose levels.
source: Indeed, one week after adenovirus administration, the acute deletion of STIM1 resulted in significantly higher fasting glucose levels (Figure 3H) without any difference in insulin levels (Figure 3I) and body weight (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by fasting glucose measurements (Figure 3H).

claim: Following acute STIM1 deletion, mice exhibited significantly impaired glucose tolerance.
source: Interestingly, following STIM1 deletion, mice also exhibited significantly impaired glucose tolerance (Figure 3J).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test (Figure 3J).

claim: Acute SOCE dysfunction in the liver results in amplified cellular stress and glucose intolerance in mice fed a HFD.
source: In summary, acute SOCE dysfunction in the liver results in amplified cellular stress and glucose intolerance in mice fed a HFD.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test and stress marker analysis in mice with acute STIM1 deletion (Figure 3G-J).

claim: The functionality of the STIM1-YFP fusion protein has been verified previously.
source: The functionality of the STIM1-YFP fusion protein has been verified previously (Liou et al., 2005) and confirmed by us (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liou et al., 2005 and Video 1.

claim: In control Lepob/ob cells expressing GFP, STIM1 formed puncta at baseline and Tg-induced translocation of the protein was impaired.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, in control Lepob/ob cells expressing GFP, STIM1 formed puncta at baseline and Tg-induced translocation of the protein was impaired, as we previously observed (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of STIM1 in Lepob/ob hepatocytes expressing adGFP (Figure 4B).

claim: Delivery of STIM1-YFP lead to a significant increase in the protein level in liver cells.
source: Delivery of STIM1-YFP lead to a significant increase in the protein level in liver cells.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 4A).

claim: In non treated cells, some degree of the STIM1 protein was already localized in areas of close contact with the plasma membrane even prior to stimulation following STIM1-YFP overexpression.
source: Interestingly, in non treated cells, we observed that some degree of the STIM1 protein was already localized in areas of close contact with the plasma membrane even prior to stimulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of STIM1 in Lepob/ob hepatocytes expressing adSTIM1-YFP (Figure 4C).

claim: Exogenously expressed STIM1 was able to translocate towards the plasma membrane after Tg treatment.
source: Additionally, exogenously expressed STIM1 was able to translocate towards the plasma membrane after Tg treatment (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of STIM1 in Lepob/ob hepatocytes expressing adSTIM1-YFP (Figure 4C and D).

claim: Exogenous delivery of STIM1-HRP resulted in rescue of translocation in cells from obese animals in a manner similar to that observed in lean, wild type cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4E, exogenous delivery of STIM1-HRP resulted in rescue of translocation in cells from obese animals in a manner similar to that observed in lean, wild type cells.
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy of STIM1-HRP in Lepob/ob hepatocytes (Figure 4E).

claim: Exogenously increasing the amount of STIM1 protein is sufficient to partially overcome the STIM1 translocation defect in cells from obese mice.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that exogenously increasing the amount of STIM1 protein is sufficient to partially overcome the STIM1 translocation defect in cells from obese mice.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging, quantification, and TEM of STIM1 in Lepob/ob hepatocytes overexpressing STIM1 (Figure 4B-E).

claim: STIM1-YFP overexpression resulted in an ~20 fold increase in the expression of STIM1 protein.
source: As shown in Figure 4F, STIM1-YFP overexpression resulted in an ~20 fold increase in the expression of STIM1 protein.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 4F).

claim: The amount of O-GlcNac modified STIM1 did not increase proportionally to total STIM1 following STIM1-YFP overexpression, indicating that a significant amount of the overexpressed STIM1 escapes this post translation modification.
source: However, the amount of O-GlcNac modified STIM1 did not increase proportionally, indicating that in fact a significant amount of the overexpressed STIM1 escapes this post translation modification.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation of O-GlcNAc-modified proteins followed by STIM1 immunoblotting (Figure 4F).

claim: Overexpression of STIM1 in HeLa cells leads to morphological changes in the ER with an increased cortical ER.
source: Additionally, it has been previously shown that overexpression of STIM1 in HeLa cells leads to morphological changes in the ER with an increased cortical ER (Orci et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Orci et al., 2009.

claim: STIM1-YFP expression led to a remodeling of ER with abundant ER stacks apposed to the PM in primary hepatocytes derived from Lepob/ob mice.
source: In agreement with this finding, electron micrographs of primary hepatocytes derived from Lepob/ob mice show that STIM1-YFP expression led to a remodeling of ER with abundant ER stacks apposed to the PM, although the degree of ER remodeling varied from cell to cell, likely due to variable STIM1 expression levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Overexpression of STIM1-YFP in Lepob/ob cells resulted in increased ER Ca2+ compared to control cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4G overexpression of STIM1-YFP in Lepob/ob cells resulted in increased ER Ca2+ and SOCE compared to control cells.
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements (Figure 4G).

claim: Overexpression of STIM1-YFP in Lepob/ob cells resulted in increased SOCE compared to control cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4G overexpression of STIM1-YFP in Lepob/ob cells resulted in increased ER Ca2+ and SOCE compared to control cells.
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium measurements (Figure 4G).

claim: Overexpression of STIM1 was a successful intervention to overcome the STIM translocation and SOCE defects, resulting in improved ER calcium handling.
source: Thus, overexpression of STIM1 was a successful intervention to overcome the STIM translocation and SOCE defects, resulting in improved ER calcium handling.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging, TEM, and calcium measurements in Lepob/ob hepatocytes overexpressing STIM1 (Figure 4).

claim: Increased STIM1 expression was accompanied by increased mRNA expression of Orai1.
source: Interestingly, increased STIM1 expression was also accompanied by increased mRNA expression of Orai1 and with an increase in SERCA (Atp2a2) mRNA and protein levels (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 5B).

claim: Increased STIM1 expression was accompanied by an increase in SERCA (Atp2a2) mRNA and protein levels.
source: Interestingly, increased STIM1 expression was also accompanied by increased mRNA expression of Orai1 and with an increase in SERCA (Atp2a2) mRNA and protein levels (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and western blot data (Figure 5B and C).

claim: Modulation of expression STIM1 affects the expression of other Ca2+ channels or pumps, as SERCA, likely due to alterations in cytosolic Ca2+ levels.
source: This is in accordance with previous work showing that the modulation of expression STIM1 affects the expression of other Ca2+ channels or pumps, as SERCA, likely due to alterations in cytosolic Ca2+ levels (Abell et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abell et al., 2011.

claim: Liver-specific overexpression of STIM1 led to a significant improvement in glucose tolerance relative to control (adGFP) animals.
source: Remarkably, liver-specific overexpression of STIM1 led to a significant improvement in glucose tolerance relative to control (adGFP) animals as evaluated by a glucose tolerance test (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test (Figure 5D).

claim: Improved glucose tolerance resulting from overexpression of STIM1 was associated with enhanced in vivo insulin signaling.
source: Improved glucose tolerance resulting from overexpression of STIM1 was associated with enhanced in vivo insulin signaling evaluated by direct insulin injection into the livers that resulted in increased AKT phosphorylation (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo insulin signaling measurements (Figure 5E).

claim: Expression of genes involved in glycolysis were increased in livers overexpressing STIM1.
source: Additionally, expression of genes involved in glycolysis were increased in livers overexpressing STIM1, accompanied by decreased levels of PCK1 (PEPCK), a rate limiting enzyme for gluconeogenesis (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 5F and G).

claim: Expression of PCK1 (PEPCK), a rate limiting enzyme for gluconeogenesis, was decreased in livers overexpressing STIM1.
source: Additionally, expression of genes involved in glycolysis were increased in livers overexpressing STIM1, accompanied by decreased levels of PCK1 (PEPCK), a rate limiting enzyme for gluconeogenesis (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 5F and G).

claim: Exogenous expression of STIM1 led to a reduction in total Tg content in the liver tissue of Lepob/ob mice compared to controls expressing GFP.
source: As shown in Figure 5H, exogenous expression of STIM1 led to a reduction in total Tg content in the liver tissue of Lepob/ob mice compared to controls expressing GFP.
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements (Figure 5H).

claim: STIM1 overexpression led to increase mRNA expression of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation, such as CPT1.
source: Accordingly, STIM1 overexpression led to increase mRNA expression of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation, such as CPT1, while no change was observed in genes involved in lipogenesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: No change was observed in genes involved in lipogenesis following STIM1 overexpression.
source: Accordingly, STIM1 overexpression led to increase mRNA expression of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation, such as CPT1, while no change was observed in genes involved in lipogenesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: SOCE is critical for glucose and lipid metabolism.
source: Based on these results we conclude that SOCE is critical for glucose and lipid metabolism and that increasing hepatic SOCE through overexpression of STIM1 is able to revert, at least in part, the deleterious impact of obesity on systemic glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing effects of STIM1 manipulation on glucose and lipid metabolism (Figure 3, 4, and 5).

claim: Increasing hepatic SOCE through overexpression of STIM1 is able to revert, at least in part, the deleterious impact of obesity on systemic glucose homeostasis.
source: Based on these results we conclude that SOCE is critical for glucose and lipid metabolism and that increasing hepatic SOCE through overexpression of STIM1 is able to revert, at least in part, the deleterious impact of obesity on systemic glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test and metabolic measurements in Lepob/ob mice overexpressing STIM1 (Figure 5).

claim: Disrupted intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis in metabolic tissues is a key component of ER dysfunction and metabolic deterioration.
source: In the last several years, a growing number of studies have laid the foundation for the concept that disrupted intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis in metabolic tissues is a key component of ER dysfunction and metabolic deterioration (Arruda and Hotamisligil, 2015; Ozcan and Tabas, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arruda and Hotamisligil, 2015 and Ozcan and Tabas, 2016.

claim: The abnormal Ca2+ handling in the ER of hepatocytes in obesity involves both impairment of SERCA activity.
source: The abnormal Ca2+ handling in the ER of hepatocytes in this setting is multi-faceted, involving both impairment of SERCA activity (Fu et al., 2011) as well as increased activity of IP3R (Arruda et al., 2014; Feriod et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fu et al., 2011.

claim: The abnormal Ca2+ handling in the ER of hepatocytes in obesity involves increased activity of IP3R.
source: The abnormal Ca2+ handling in the ER of hepatocytes in this setting is multi-faceted, involving both impairment of SERCA activity (Fu et al., 2011) as well as increased activity of IP3R (Arruda et al., 2014; Feriod et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arruda et al., 2014; Feriod et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2012.

claim: SNPs in SERCA are associated with metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes.
source: Supporting the critical role of this biology, human genetic studies have shown that SNPs in SERCA (Varadi et al., 1999) and IP3R (Shungin et al., 2015) are associated with metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Varadi et al., 1999.

claim: SNPs in IP3R are associated with metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes.
source: Supporting the critical role of this biology, human genetic studies have shown that SNPs in SERCA (Varadi et al., 1999) and IP3R (Shungin et al., 2015) are associated with metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shungin et al., 2015.

claim: STIM-mediated SOCE is defective in obesity with important implications for the metabolic dysfunction in hepatocytes.
source: Here, our work reveals that another key mechanism supporting ER Ca2+ homeostasis, STIM-mediated SOCE, is also defective in obesity with important implications for the metabolic dysfunction in hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging, confocal imaging, and metabolic measurements throughout the manuscript (Figures 1-5).

claim: STIM1 gain-of-function improves cellular stress responses and glucose homeostasis in obese mice.
source: Strikingly, we demonstrate that STIM1 gain-of-function improves cellular stress responses and glucose homeostasis in obese mice, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting Ca2+ homeostasis through STIM1 for metabolic disease treatment.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test and metabolic measurements in Lepob/ob mice overexpressing STIM1 (Figure 5).

claim: Protein modification with O-GlcNAc is a reflection of the nutritional status, as it integrates glucose, amino acid, fatty acid and nucleotide flux through the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP) to produce N-acetyl-glucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), the obligatory substrate for OGT.
source: Regardless, protein modification with O-GlcNAc is a reflection of the nutritional status, as it integrates glucose, amino acid, fatty acid and nucleotide flux through the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP) to produce N-acetyl-glucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), the obligatory substrate for OGT.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about O-GlcNAcylation.

claim: Conditions of nutrient and substrate excess, including obesity, lead to increased cellular O-GlcNAcylation levels.
source: Hence, conditions of nutrient and substrate excess, including obesity, lead to increased cellular O-GlcNAcylation levels (Vosseller et al., 2002; Yang and Qian, 2017; Dentin et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vosseller et al., 2002; Yang and Qian, 2017; Dentin et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008.

claim: O-GlcNAc modification of STIM1 alters organelle Ca2+ regulation with consequences for ER function and systemic metabolism.
source: Taken together, our findings demonstrate that O-GlcNAc modification of STIM1 alters organelle Ca2+ regulation with consequences for ER function and systemic metabolism and provide an important mechanistic insight into regulation of this critical metabolic integration point through organelle homeostasis in obesity.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing O-GlcNAcylation of STIM1, its effects on STIM1 function, and metabolic consequences (Figure 2-5).

claim: Cells from patients with loss-of-function mutations in STIM1 or ORAI accumulate lipid droplets as a consequence of their inability to increase cAMP, mobilize fatty acids from lipid droplets, activate lipolysis, and oxidize fatty acids.
source: Recently, it has been reported that cells from patients with loss-of-function mutations in STIM1 or ORAI accumulate lipid droplets as a consequence of their inability to increase cAMP, mobilize fatty acids from lipid droplets, activate lipolysis, and oxidize fatty acids (Maus et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maus et al., 2017.

claim: Hepatocyte-specific deletion of STIM1 led to a mild metabolic phenotype in vivo suggesting that the activation of compensatory systems occurs when STIM1 is deleted during development.
source: Hepatocyte-specific deletion of STIM1 led to a mild metabolic phenotype in vivo suggesting that the activation of compensatory systems occurs when STIM1 is deleted during development.
evidence: Supported by metabolic measurements in stim1ΔLIVER mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and logical inference.

claim: STIM2 expression levels were slightly increased in STIM1 deficient liver.
source: Indeed, STIM2 expression levels were slightly increased in STIM1 deficient liver.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Acute down-regulation of STIM1 showed a more marked effect on glucose homeostasis than constitutive deletion.
source: In contrast, acute down-regulation of STIM1 showed a more marked effect on glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by comparison of metabolic phenotypes in constitutive (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) versus acute (Figure 3H-J) STIM1 deletion.

claim: Overexpression of STIM1 in hepatocytes from Lepob/ob animals led to remodeling of the ER with an increase in the amount of cortical ER possibly facilitating STIM1 translocation and Orai1 coupling.
source: Additionally, overexpression of STIM1 in hepatocytes from Lepob/ob animals led to remodeling of the ER with an increase in the amount of cortical ER possibly facilitating STIM1 translocation and Orai1 coupling.
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and logical inference.

claim: STIM1 regulates the structure of the ER through its role in Tip Attachment Complex movement, coordinating the growth and shrinkage of the ER tubule.
source: Indeed, it is known that STIM1 regulates the structure of the ER through its role in Tip Attachment Complex movement (Grigoriev et al., 2008; Westrate et al., 2015), coordinating the growth and shrinkage of the ER tubule.
evidence: Supported by citations to Grigoriev et al., 2008 and Westrate et al., 2015.

claim: In T cells SOCE regulates the expression of glycolytic genes through the modulation of the transcription factor NFAT.
source: This is in agreement with recent report showing that in T cells SOCE regulates the expression of glycolytic genes through the modulation of the transcription factor NFAT (Vaeth et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vaeth et al., 2017.

claim: An adaptive feedback loop between components of Ca2+ machinery exist to keep cytosolic Ca2+ levels under control.
source: In fact, it is proposed and validated experimentally and computationally that an adaptive feedback loop between components of Ca2+ machinery exist to keep cytosolic Ca2+ levels under control (Abell et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abell et al., 2011.

claim: Increased SERCA expression in the context of STIM1 overexpression may be a critical component of the metabolic benefit resulting from STIM1 expression in the liver in obese mice.
source: Increased SERCA expression in the context of STIM1 overexpression may indeed be a critical component of the metabolic benefit resulting from STIM1 expression in the liver in obese mice.
evidence: Supported by western blot and qPCR data showing increased SERCA expression (Figure 5B and C) and logical inference.

claim: Individual manipulation of multiple proteins involved in the maintenance of ER Ca2+ levels- SERCA, IP3R, and STIM1- all result in a similar phenotype.
source: It is remarkable that the individual manipulation of multiple proteins involved in the maintenance of ER Ca2+ levels- SERCA, IP3R, and STIM1- all result in a similar phenotype.
evidence: Supported by comparison of phenotypes from this study and cited literature on SERCA and IP3R manipulation.

claim: ER Ca2+ homeostasis and ER function are important to metabolic health.
source: These findings underscore the importance of ER Ca2+ homeostasis and ER function to metabolic health, and indicate the strong potential for targeting these pathways to combat metabolic disease.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript showing effects of ER Ca2+ homeostasis on metabolism (Figures 1-5).

claim: There is strong potential for targeting ER Ca2+ homeostasis pathways to combat metabolic disease.
source: These findings underscore the importance of ER Ca2+ homeostasis and ER function to metabolic health, and indicate the strong potential for targeting these pathways to combat metabolic disease.
evidence: Supported by the beneficial effects of STIM1 overexpression on glucose tolerance in obese mice (Figure 5) and logical inference.
